description.value: The study investigated neural activation to visual cannabis cues compared with matched non-cannabis cues in regular cannabis-using youth.

value: It was hypothesized that cannabis cues, relative to non-cannabis cues, would elicit activation in reward-related brain regions such as the orbitofrontal cortex and ventral striatum.
activation would be positively associated with measures of cannabis dependence and quantity/frequency of cannabis use.
no significant activation differences would emerge between passive and active cannabis cues.
cannabis cues (both active and passive) were expected to be subjectively rated by adolescent users as more rewarding than non-cannabis cues

spans.text: During the task, participants in the scanner were shown pseudorandomly interspersed cannabis and non-cannabis images, visual control images (i.e., blurred images), and a fixation cross ( ).

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to press the button corresponding to their urge rating during the task. During each urge-rating period, they rated their cannabis craving.

spans.text: While in the scanner, participants were given instructions for completing the task (i.e., pressing the button corresponding to their urge rating, see Supplement 1).

stimuli.value: Thirty-six high-resolution cannabis images, matched individually to 36 non-cannabis images on color, hue, and visual complexity. Non-cannabis images depicted non-food objects or plants. Cannabis images included 12 active scenes depicting someone smoking or handling cannabis or paraphernalia and 24 passive scenes depicting only paraphernalia or a cannabis plant. Blurred control images and fixation crosses were also presented.

spans.text: 36 cannabis stimuli were matched by color, hue, and visual complexity to 36 non-cannabis images (i.e., each cannabis image was matched to a specific non-cannabis image on these dimensions, resulting in 36 matched cannabis/non-cannabis image pairs).
